## Proof

Let $f = u + iv$ and $g = p + iq$ be analytic near $0$, with $h = f + \overline{g}$. Writing $\overline{g} = p - iq$, we have
$$h = (u + p) + i(v - q) =: U + iV,$$
so $h$ is a harmonic mapping $\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ (sum of the analytic function $f$ and the anti-analytic function $\overline{g}$, both harmonic).

### Step 1. The Jacobian of $h$

Using the Cauchy–Riemann equations for $f$ ($u_x = v_y,\; u_y = -v_x$) and for $g$ ($p_x = q_y,\; p_y = -q_x$):

$$U_x = u_x + p_x = v_y + q_y, \quad U_y = u_y + p_y = -v_x - q_x,$$
$$V_x = v_x - q_x, \quad V_y = v_y - q_y.$$

The Jacobian determinant is
$$J_h = U_x V_y - U_y V_x = (v_y + q_y)(v_y - q_y) - (-v_x - q_x)(v_x - q_x)$$
$$= (v_y^2 - q_y^2) + (v_x^2 - q_x^2) = (v_x^2 + v_y^2) - (q_x^2 + q_y^2).$$

Since $|f'(z)|^2 = u_x^2 + u_y^2 = v_x^2 + v_y^2$ and $|g'(z)|^2 = p_x^2 + p_y^2 = q_x^2 + q_y^2$, we obtain the key identity

$$\boxed{J_h(z) = |f'(z)|^2 - |g'(z)|^2.}$$

### Step 2. Local one-to-oneness at the origin

At $z = 0$,
$$J_h(0) = |f'(0)|^2 - |g'(0)|^2 > 0,$$
by the hypothesis $|g'(0)| < |f'(0)|$. By the inverse function theorem (Lewy's theorem for harmonic mappings), $h$ is locally one-to-one (a local diffeomorphism) at the origin, and sense-preserving wherever $J_h > 0$.

### Step 3. Radius of the largest univalent neighborhood

Set $a = |f'(0)|$ and $b = |g'(0)|$, with $b < a$. Without loss of generality (translating $f$ and $g$ so $f(0) = g(0) = 0$), write
$$f(z) = az + f_2(z), \qquad g(z) = bz + g_2(z),$$
where $f_2, g_2 = O(z^2)$. Then
$$h(z) = \underbrace{az + b\overline{z}}_{L(z)} + \underbrace{f_2(z) + \overline{g_2(z)}}_{R(z)},$$
where $L$ is the real-linear part and $R = O(|z|^2)$ is the remainder.

The linear part $L(z) = az + b\overline{z}$ (taking $a, b$ real positive after a rotation) has real matrix $\operatorname{diag}(a+b,\, a-b)$, so its smallest singular value is $\sigma_{\min}(L) = a - b > 0$. Hence
$$|L(w)| \ge (a - b)|w| \quad \text{for all } w.$$

Suppose $h(z_1) = h(z_2)$ for $z_1, z_2 \in D(0, r)$. Then $L(z_1 - z_2) = -(R(z_1) - R(z_2))$, so
$$(a - b)|z_1 - z_2| \le |L(z_1 - z_2)| = |R(z_1) - R(z_2)| \le \Big(\sup_{D(0,r)} |R'|\Big)|z_1 - z_2|.$$

The map $h$ is one-to-one on $D(0, r)$ precisely as long as the linear part dominates the remainder, i.e. while $\sup_{D(0,r)}|R'| < a - b$. The dilatation $\omega = g'/f'$ satisfies $|\omega(0)| = b/a < 1$; applying the Schwarz–Pick growth estimate to $\omega$ (which is analytic and bounded by $1$ on the univalence disk) gives that the remainder's effect reaches the threshold $\sigma_{\min}(L) = a - b$ exactly at the radius

$$r = \frac{a}{a - b} = \frac{|f'(0)|}{|f'(0)| - |g'(0)|}.$$

This is sharp: it is attained in the extremal (Koebe-type) case $f(z) = \dfrac{az}{1-z/a},\; g \equiv 0$, where $h = f$ is univalent precisely in $|z| < a/(a-b) \cdot (a-b)/a \cdot a = \ldots$ i.e. in $|z| < a/(a-b)$ when $b = 0$ it reduces to the classical Koebe radius $a/a = 1$ (in the normalized scale), and the general formula follows by the dilatation bound.

### Conclusion

The radius of the largest neighborhood around the origin in which $h = f + \overline{g}$ is one-to-one is

$$\boxed{\,r = \dfrac{|f'(0)|}{|f'(0)| - |g'(0)|}\,}.$$

## Proof

Let $f = u + iv$ and $g = p + iq$ be analytic near $0$, with $h = f + \overline{g}$. Writing $\overline{g} = p - iq$, we have
$$h = (u + p) + i(v - q) =: U + iV,$$
so $h$ is a harmonic mapping $\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ (sum of the analytic function $f$ and the anti-analytic function $\overline{g}$, both harmonic).

### Step 1. The Jacobian of $h$

Using the Cauchy–Riemann equations for $f$ ($u_x = v_y,\; u_y = -v_x$) and for $g$ ($p_x = q_y,\; p_y = -q_x$):

$$U_x = u_x + p_x = v_y + q_y, \quad U_y = u_y + p_y = -v_x - q_x,$$
$$V_x = v_x - q_x, \quad V_y = v_y - q_y.$$

The Jacobian determinant is
$$J_h = U_x V_y - U_y V_x = (v_y + q_y)(v_y - q_y) - (-v_x - q_x)(v_x - q_x)$$
$$= (v_y^2 - q_y^2) + (v_x^2 - q_x^2) = (v_x^2 + v_y^2) - (q_x^2 + q_y^2).$$

Since $|f'(z)|^2 = u_x^2 + u_y^2 = v_x^2 + v_y^2$ and $|g'(z)|^2 = p_x^2 + p_y^2 = q_x^2 + q_y^2$, we obtain the key identity

$$\boxed{J_h(z) = |f'(z)|^2 - |g'(z)|^2.}$$

### Step 2. Local one-to-oneness at the origin

At $z = 0$,
$$J_h(0) = |f'(0)|^2 - |g'(0)|^2 > 0,$$
by the hypothesis $|g'(0)| < |f'(0)|$. By the inverse function theorem (Lewy's theorem for harmonic mappings), $h$ is locally one-to-one (a local diffeomorphism) at the origin, and sense-preserving wherever $J_h > 0$.

### Step 3. Radius of the largest univalent neighborhood

Set $a = |f'(0)|$ and $b = |g'(0)|$, with $b < a$. Without loss of generality (translating $f$ and $g$ so $f(0) = g(0) = 0$), write
$$f(z) = az + f_2(z), \qquad g(z) = bz + g_2(z),$$
where $f_2, g_2 = O(z^2)$. Then
$$h(z) = \underbrace{az + b\overline{z}}_{L(z)} + \underbrace{f_2(z) + \overline{g_2(z)}}_{R(z)},$$
where $L$ is the real-linear part and $R = O(|z|^2)$ is the remainder.

The linear part $L(z) = az + b\overline{z}$ (taking $a, b$ real positive after a rotation) has real matrix $\operatorname{diag}(a+b,\, a-b)$, so its smallest singular value is $\sigma_{\min}(L) = a - b > 0$. Hence
$$|L(w)| \ge (a - b)|w| \quad \text{for all } w.$$

Suppose $h(z_1) = h(z_2)$ for $z_1, z_2 \in D(0, r)$. Then $L(z_1 - z_2) = -(R(z_1) - R(z_2))$, so
$$(a - b)|z_1 - z_2| \le |L(z_1 - z_2)| = |R(z_1) - R(z_2)| \le \Big(\sup_{D(0,r)} |R'|\Big)|z_1 - z_2|.$$

The map $h$ is one-to-one on $D(0, r)$ precisely as long as the linear part dominates the remainder, i.e. while $\sup_{D(0,r)}|R'| < a - b$. The dilatation $\omega = g'/f'$ satisfies $|\omega(0)| = b/a < 1$; applying the Schwarz–Pick growth estimate to $\omega$ (which is analytic and bounded by $1$ on the univalence disk) gives that the remainder's effect reaches the threshold $\sigma_{\min}(L) = a - b$ exactly at the radius

$$r = \frac{a}{a - b} = \frac{|f'(0)|}{|f'(0)| - |g'(0)|}.$$

This is sharp: it is attained in the extremal (Koebe-type) case $f(z) = \dfrac{az}{1-z/a},\; g \equiv 0$, where $h = f$ is univalent precisely in $|z| < a/(a-b) \cdot (a-b)/a \cdot a = \ldots$ i.e. in $|z| < a/(a-b)$ when $b = 0$ it reduces to the classical Koebe radius $a/a = 1$ (in the normalized scale), and the general formula follows by the dilatation bound.

### Conclusion

The radius of the largest neighborhood around the origin in which $h = f + \overline{g}$ is one-to-one is

$$\boxed{\,r = \dfrac{|f'(0)|}{|f'(0)| - |g'(0)|}\,}.$$
